lines.text: Every satellite signal reaches the ground buried in natural noise.
A careful attacker can shape an attack to look exactly like that noise.
This is how it works, and how our ground-link testbed still catches it.
Our satellite flies at 542.8 km and sends a fixed X-band carrier at 8477.8 MHz.
lines.say: Our satellite sends a fixed X band carrier, at eight thousand, four hundred and seventy-seven point eight megahertz.

lines.text: The frequency is not random: it moves only with the Doppler shift, up to ±198 kHz, which the orbit predicts.
lines.say: The frequency is not random. It moves only with the Doppler shift, up to about two hundred kilohertz either way, and the orbit predicts it.

lines.text: At Zaghouan the carrier arrives between −88 and −75 dBm: an amplitude of 12.5 to 57 µV.
lines.say: At Zagwan, it arrives between minus eighty-eight and minus seventy-five D B M: an amplitude of twelve and a half to fifty-seven microvolts.

lines.text: The receiver's noise floor is −100 dBm, so the signal-to-noise ratio runs from 12 to 25 dB over the pass.
lines.say: The noise floor is minus one hundred D B M, so the signal-to-noise ratio runs from twelve to twenty-five decibels.

lines.text: Natural noise has a signature.
Thermal noise is Gaussian and white: a flat floor across the band.
Against the orbit model, the carrier wanders by less than 20 Hz and the power by less than 1 dB.
lines.say: Against the orbit model, the carrier wanders by less than twenty hertz, and the power by less than one decibel.

lines.text: That narrow envelope is where an attacker has to hide.
One: noise-shaped jamming. Gaussian noise, raised slowly like a rain fade, so the floor creeps up instead of jumping.
Two: fade-mimicking spoofing. A rogue node matches the Doppler and adds fake fading, so its power sits only 3 dB low.
lines.say: Two: fade-mimicking spoofing. A rogue node matches the Doppler and adds fake fading, so its power sits only three decibels low.

lines.text: Three: bit flips disguised as channel errors. Chosen bits are flipped and the checksum recomputed, so the frame just looks noisy.
Our idea is to make every imitation either harmless or visible.
Layer one is physics. To stay hidden, the injected noise can be at most 1.8 dB above the thermal noise: that costs at most 4 dB of signal-to-noise ratio, and every frame still verifies.
lines.say: Layer one is physics. To stay hidden, the injected noise can be at most one point eight decibels above the thermal noise. That costs at most four decibels, and every frame still verifies.

lines.text: Push harder, and the physics gate fires.
Layer two is an Isolation Forest trained only on clean passes.
It scores each reading together with how fast it changed, so a disguise must copy the rhythm of nature, not just its level.
Layer three is cryptography, which noise cannot imitate: every frame carries an HMAC-SHA256 tag made with a secret key.
lines.say: Layer three is cryptography, which noise cannot imitate. Every frame carries an H MAC tag, made with a secret key.

lines.text: Change one bit, by accident or on purpose, and the tag breaks: the frame is dropped and requested again.
One failure looks like weather. A burst of failures trips two of our three detectors, and the link is quarantined.
In our tests, every attack packet was denied, and no corrupted frame reached the analyst.
About one percent of genuine packets were held back.
Try it live at tsyp-pi.vercel.app.
lines.say: Try it live, on our testbed.
